# State of Columbia — Child Support Guidelines (income shares) — worksheet excerpt

*Citation:* Col. Rev. Stat. §14-10-115 (fictional); Worksheet A  
*Status in this library:* in force

**Income.** Gross income includes salary, wages, commissions, **bonuses** (including expected or recurring bonuses evidenced by employer documents), and other income. **Net income** for the worksheet = gross income × 0.78 (standardized deduction for taxes/FICA), ÷ 12.
**Basic obligation (two children), by combined monthly net income:** ≤5,000: 1,180 · ≤7,500: 1,640 · ≤10,000: 2,010 · ≤12,500: 2,330 · ≤15,000: 2,600 · ≤20,000: 3,050 · ≤25,000: 3,380.

**Maintenance** paid between the parties is added to the recipient's and subtracted from the payor's income before computing support.

# Filing status; dependents of divorced parents; Form 8332

*Citation:* IRC §§2(b), 7703(a), 152(e); Form 8332  
*Status in this library:* in force

Marital status is determined on **December 31**; a decree final on or before that date → each files single or head of household. **Head of household** requires a qualifying child living with the taxpayer more than half the year and payment of more than half the cost of the home. **§152(e):** the custodial parent (more nights) claims the child unless the custodial parent releases the claim on **Form 8332**; the release moves the child tax credit but **not** head-of-household status, EITC or the dependent-care credit, which stay with the custodial parent.

# IRC §§1041, 121(d)(3), 71/215 (post-TCJA) — divorce tax rules

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §1041; §121(b)(1), (d)(3); TCJA §11051 (P.L. 115-97)  
*Status in this library:* in force

**§1041:** no gain or loss on transfers between spouses or former spouses incident to divorce; the transferee takes the transferor's basis (carryover). **§121:** exclusion of gain on sale of a principal residence: $250,000 (single) / $500,000 (joint return) if owned and used as principal residence 2 of the last 5 years. **§121(d)(3)(A):** an individual is treated as using property as a principal residence during any period of ownership while the individual's spouse or former spouse is granted use under a divorce instrument. **(B):** property transferred to an individual incident to divorce includes the transferor's ownership period. **Alimony (TCJA):** for divorce or separation instruments executed after December 31, 2018, alimony is **neither deductible by the payor nor includible by the recipient**. Child support is never deductible or includible.

# Retirement plan division — QDRO; early-distribution penalty exception

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §414(p); §72(t)(2)(C); ERISA §206(d)(3)  
*Status in this library:* in force

A division of a qualified plan (401(k)) between spouses must be made by a **qualified domestic relations order**; absent a QDRO, a distribution to the participant to pay the former spouse is taxable to the participant and, if under 59½, subject to the 10% additional tax. Distributions to an alternate payee **under a QDRO** are exempt from the §72(t) 10% penalty (§72(t)(2)(C)) and are taxed to the alternate payee; the alternate payee may roll over to an IRA. An IRA is divided by transfer incident to divorce without a QDRO (§408(d)(6)).

# Advice for Wife — the proposed "equal halves" division and support

**Bottom line: the proposal is not 50/50.** Nominally it is ($770,000 each), but after tax Wife receives about **$613,008 vs Husband's $662,000** — 7.4% less. It also (a) understates child support by using a salary that hides a documented $45,000 bonus, (b) misstates the tax treatment of maintenance, and (c) gives away your claim to the children. There is real negotiation leverage because Husband signed an affidavit denying a bonus his own employer had already promised him.

Everything below is grounded only in the reference library (`library/INDEX.md`); anything marked **[unverified]** is not covered by the library and must be checked.

## 1. Why "equal halves" is not equal after tax

Tax follows the asset, not the label (§1041 transfers are tax-free and the transferee takes the transferor's basis — `library/irc_1041_121_71.md`):

| Item | Nominal | Embedded tax | After-tax |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| **Husband's side** | | | |
| 401(k), pre-tax | 400,000 | ordinary rates on withdrawal; assumed 24% | 304,000 |
| Brokerage (gain 80,000) | 300,000 | 15% LTCG = 12,000 | 288,000 |
| Cash | 50,000 | — | 50,000 |
| Tacoma | 20,000 | — | 20,000 |
| **Husband total** | **770,000** | | **662,000** |
| **Wife's side** | | | |
| House equity | 700,000 | selling 6% (66,000) + cap-gains tax below | 543,008 |
| Cash | 50,000 | — | 50,000 |
| Volvo | 20,000 | — | 20,000 |
| **Wife total** | **770,000** | | **613,008** |

House tax if sold today: gain = 1,100,000 − 66,000 selling costs − 300,000 carryover basis = **734,000**; your single §121 exclusion is **250,000**, leaving 484,000 taxed at 15% LTCG + 3.8% NIIT = **90,992** (the engagement's conservative NIIT assumption, and it is well founded here: the gain alone puts MAGI far above the $200,000 single NIIT threshold). Net house dollars: 700,000 − 66,000 − 90,992 = **543,008**.

**Gap: 662,000 − 613,008 = 48,992 in Husband's favor**, before counting the hidden bonus (Section 2). Sensitivity on Husband's 401(k) rate (engagement assumption, 24%): at 12% his side is 710,000 (gap 96,992); at 32% his side is 630,000 (gap 16,992). Under every setting, Wife is short.

Also note the schedule itself is missing an asset: the bonus (next section) is compensation earned during the marriage and belongs in the pot.

## 2. The undisclosed bonus — use it

- Sworn affidavit (2026-08-30): bonus "discretionary; none expected for 2026."
- Employer letter (2026-03-02, **predating the affidavit**): 2026 target bonus **$45,000**, half paid September, half February; he was "at 112% of plan" → expected payout ≈ $45,000 × 1.12 = **$50,400**.
- Pay stub (2026-09-15): YTD gross 146,212 vs 119,000 prorated salary → **+$27,212 unexplained**, roughly matching the September half (25,200 at 112%; ~$2,012 still unexplained).

Columbia counts expected, employer-documented bonuses as income (`library/columbia_child_support_guidelines.md`) and requires full disclosure of bonuses in the sworn affidavit; a party who fails to disclose **may have the judgment reopened and may be sanctioned, including an unequal division in the other party's favor** (`library/columbia_equitable_distribution.md`, Col. R. Fam. P. 16.2(e)). Ask the court to include the bonus in the estate (at target 45,000, or at 112% if the plan confirms) and account for the Feb-2027 half, which is on no schedule. The disclosure failure is also your leverage to press for the after-tax equalization in Section 1.

## 3. Maintenance: his stated tax treatment is wrong — in your favor

For a decree signed after 12/31/2018, alimony is **neither deductible by the payor nor taxable to the recipient** (TCJA §11051; `library/irc_1041_121_71.md`). The proposal's "deductible to Husband and taxable to Wife" is a drafting error (he appears to be pricing 2018 law). Fix the decree language: the $2,000/month is tax-free to you and un-deductible by him — so $2,000/month for 36 months ($72,000) costs him more than he thinks. Child support is never deductible or includible. Do **not** let him "gross up" or shrink maintenance on the theory that he loses a deduction he never had — but note the Columbia worksheet still adds maintenance to your income and subtracts it from his when computing child support, which trims his support number slightly (Section 4).

## 4. Child support should be higher than he proposes

## 5. The house — the keep-it goal has a hard problem

Selling now captures the $500,000 exclusion; that is worth ~$47,000 and should be on the table.

## 6. Instruments you need

- **QDRO** for any split of the 401(k) — without one, a payoff to you is taxed to *him* and, if he is under 59½, hit with the 10% penalty; a proper QDRO moves the tax to you and the 10% penalty does **not** apply to your QDRO distributions (§414(p), §72(t)(2)(C), ERISA §206(d)(3); `library/qdro_72t.md`). Get the QDRO entered with the decree, and decide whether you'll roll your share to an IRA (penalty-free after 59½; before 59½ a QDRO cash-out is penalty-free but taxable — plan so you don't strand money or trip ordinary tax at 22–24% **[unverified** rate for you, not in library]).
- **Quitclaim/deed** for the house incident to divorce — tax-free, carryover basis (§1041).
- **Corrected maintenance clause** (Section 3) and a **bonus-accounting term** (Section 2).
- **Form 8332 discipline** (Section 7) and life-insurance/secured-support protections for the 36-month maintenance tail. **[unverified]** — security devices are not in the library; standard practice.
- Note: the 401(k) is marital (accrued entirely during marriage) — its nominal $400,000 is only ~$304,000 after tax, so "equal" nominal shares of cash vs 401(k) are unequal; price the 401(k) at ~76¢ on the dollar at the table.

## 7. Children and filing status — keep the claims

Under §152(e) **you** (the custodial parent — more overnights) claim both children by default; Husband's "alternating years" plan only works if **you** sign Form 8332, and that release moves **only the child tax credit** — head-of-household status, EITC, and the dependent-care credit stay with you regardless (§§2(b), 7703(a), 152(e); Form 8332; `library/filing_status_dependents.md`). Refuse the alternating-claim term, or sell it — the credit's dollar value is **not in the library [unverified]**, so price it from current law before conceding. You will likely file **head of household** (children with you more than half the year; you must pay more than half the home's costs — confirm once Husband stops contributing). Watch the Dec-31 status rule when timing the decree and any house sale.

## 8. Recommended path (numbers in `division.json`)

- **Scenario A (fits your goal):** you keep the house; a **QDRO of ~$32,232** equalizes after tax (48,992 ÷ (2 × 0.76)); add the bonus at after-tax value (45,000 × 0.76 = 34,200 → +17,100 each). Result ≈ **$654,604 each**, plus ~$4,023/month cash (maintenance + support) while it lasts.
- **Scenario B (best money):** sell the house before the Dec-31 cutoff for the **$500,000 joint exclusion**; divide the after-tax estate (1,356,208) equally with a **QDRO of ~$134,211**. Result ≈ **$678,104 each** — and you buy or rent a home you can actually carry. Ask yourself honestly whether the middle-school goal survives Scenario B's ~$47,000 premium and the refinance math.
- **Scenario C (leverage, not a demand):** an unequal division is an authorized sanction for the affidavit violation (Rule 16.2(e)); a 55/45 of the Scenario-B estate would put you at 745,914 vs 610,294. Use the exposure to get A or B, not as your opening position.

## 9. Assumptions on the record

Husband's 401(k) withdrawals taxed at 24% (sensitivity 12%/32% shown); 15% LTCG and 3.8% NIIT per the engagement convention; brokerage gains assumed long-term (**[unverified]** — the schedule says "mostly 2024–25 purchases," so some gains may be short-term at ordinary rates — ask for lot dates); selling costs 6%; refi proxy uses the existing 6.1%/24-year terms (new rate unknown); the $100,000 schedule cash may or may not already include the September bonus payment — **open item, see `QUESTIONS.md`**; the February 2027 half-bonus (~$22,500–$25,200) is unlisted either way. Nothing here relies on any authority outside `library/INDEX.md`.
